yea.e: From Middle English ye, ȝea, ya, ȝa, from Old English ġēa, iā (“yea, yes”), from Proto-West Germanic *jā. The modern pronunciation shows an irregular development of Early Modern English /ɛː/ to /eɪ/ in the standard language, probably from association with the antonym nay.

year.e: From Middle English yeer, yere, from Old English ġēar (“year”), from Proto-West Germanic *jār, from Proto-Germanic *jērą (“year”), from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, spring”).
year.g: A period of time akin to the time taken for the Earth to undergo a full cycle of seasons.

year-old.e: The combining form -year-old dates from Middle English (ȝeer old(e), yeer old(e), yere old(e)).
year-old.g: Of the age of one year.

yearly.e: From Middle English yeerly, yerely, from Old English ġēarlīċ, ġērlīċ (“yearly, of the year, annual”), equivalent to year + -ly (adjectival suffix) or -ly (adverbial suffix).

yearn.e: Probably either: a variant of earn (“to curdle, as milk”) (though this word is attested later), from Middle English erne, ernen (“to coagulate, congeal”) (chiefly South Midlands), a metathetic variant of rennen (“to run; to coagulate, congeal”), from Old English rinnan (“to run”) (with the variants iernan, irnan) and Old Norse rinna (“to move quickly, run.
yearn.g: Of milk: to curdle, especially in the cheesemaking process.

yearning.e: From Middle English yerning, from Old English ġierning, ġierninge. Equivalent to the gerund (yearn + -ing). yearn comes from Proto-West Germanic *girnijan, from Proto-Germanic *girnijaną, from *gernaz (“eager, willing”) + *-janą, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to yearn for”). By surface analysis, yearn + -ing.

yell.e: From Middle English ȝellen, yellen, from Old English ġiellan, from Proto-Germanic *gellaną.
yell.g: To shout; holler; make a loud sound with the voice, especially to express intense emotions such as anger or excitement.

yell.e: Borrowed from Scots yeld (“ceasing to give milk”).

yelling.e: From Middle English yellynge, ȝellynge; equivalent to yell + -ing.
yelling.g: The act of producing a yell.

yellow.e: From Middle English yelwe, yelou, from Old English ġeolwe, oblique form of Old English ġeolu, from Proto-West Germanic *gelu, from Proto-Germanic *gelwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃wós, from *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”). Not related to Italian giallo—see galbinus.
yellow.g: The color of sunflower petals and lemons; the color obtained by mixing green and red light, or by subtracting blue from white light; the col

yellow.e: From the colors used on traffic lights; yellow being the one for warning vehicles to stop soon.
yellow.g: Used to indicate that the speaker needs a temporary break from current sexual activity.

yes.e: From Middle English yes, from Old English ġīese (“by all means, of course, yes”), derived from the same root as yea.
yes.g: Used to show agreement or acceptance.

yesterday.e: From Middle English yesterday, yisterday, ȝesterdai, ȝisterdai, from Old English ġiestrandæġ, ġister dæġ, ġestor dæġ, ġeostran dæġ (“yesterday”), by surface analysis, yester- + day.
yesterday.g: The day immediately before today; one day ago.

yesternight.e: From Middle English yesternyght, yisternight, from Old English ġiestranniht (“yesternight”), equivalent to yester- + night.

yet.e: From Middle English yet, yit, from Old English ġīet, gȳta, from Proto-West Germanic *jūta, from Proto-Germanic *juta (compare West Frisian jit, jitte (“yet”), Dutch ooit (“ever”), German jetzt (“now”)), compound of (1) *ju (“already”, adverb).
yet.g: Thus far; up to the present; up to some unspecified time.

yet.e: From Middle English yeten, from Old English ġēotan (“to flow, pour”), from Proto-West Germanic *geutan, from Proto-Germanic *geutaną (“to flow, pour”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd- (“to pour”).
